title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(psych)
library(ordinal)
library(ggeffects)
library(broom)
library(gt)






This bfi data highlights the Big Five Personality index, with 5 personality traits/behaviours in each (25 total). Data was collected from 2800 people. Questions were answered on a 6-point Likert scale from Very inaccurate to Very accurate.
The chosen trait is Extraversion. The ordered outcome is part of Extraversion, E4, “Make Friends easily.” The predictor is a person’s Agreeableness subscale score, the mean of A1 to A5 with A1 reverse-keyed.
I predict that as people are more agreeable, that they will make friends more easily. I expect that the predictor of Agreeableness will be positively associated with higher scores in the ability to predict friends. This is because the trait of agreeableness centers around friendliness and getting along well with others, which is conducive to making friends easily.





[1] 4.653816


The N analyzed was the number of participants left after removing those with improper (incomplete/missing) data for E4. This number was N = 2791. The predictor was scored being the mean of 5 Agreeableness behaviours in the questionnaire, with A1 reverse scored and A2-A5 staying the same. The rest were scored from 106 with lower values representing less of the behavior. The mean was calculated with mean(data$agree), which was 4.65.

text:
2.2. How Predictor Relates to the Outcome

Jittered Dot Plots









The pattern that is seen is higher density in that category and data that reflects those with high agreeableness responding that it is very and moderately accurate that they are easily able to make new friends. This is a good model to use, as the data being used is categorical and is separated based on specific levels of the data representing traits. Using a decimal average is not representative of one of the six Likert categories that were provided as an option of response, as they are not categories to be averaged, or having a meaning of numerical values.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
2.3. An Unordered Outcome









As previously mentioned, the dominant trait for each participant is the trait out of the five that has the overall highest subscale scoare. This plot shows how many people have each trait as their most dominant. This graph being unordered reflects the fact that these Big Five traits (Agreeableness, Openness, etc.) carry no innate ordeer and do not mean more than the others in any way. As such, the graph is ordered from most to least commomly dominant trait (top to bottom); this is dissimilar to the ordinal, Likert scale. We would be using a multinomial model here.

Here, we are calculating cumulative probabilities, which are the probabilities of responding of a specific category (in this case, j), or something lower (i.e. selecting moderately inaccurate would also include what is below, such as very inaccurate); therefore, having 6 categories, this means that there are 5 cumulative probabilities and the sixth, adding all together would be 100%. This is why the last category would have undefined odds, becasue it incorporates everything above it. We are using these cumulative thresholds to later turn into probabilities. We will be using the function cumsum() to add these.
In order to compute these, we can split our scale in two at j, quantifying things as above or below j, allowing for the values to now become binary (before versus after) and can use other link functions such as the logit link function. This threshold is only 5 values, as it’s between each of the 6 categories to make the groupings, and there is a predetermined order that the values/outcomes will remain in.

Keeping in mind that ordinal models have no fixed value between the ordered categories, and rather it relates to falling above or below certain categories as we’ve mentioned with j above, and these are specific thresholds as the categories move between one another.

Why Center the Predictor? We will also center the mean, such that it becomes zero and all points can show variation around that. This alters the thresholds that we use to better assess the data. This also removes the ability of someone scoring a 0 on the 1-6 scale, which would also negatively impact analysis. This, however does not change the slope, in which the coefficients can show latent logit scale of agreeableness. This does not change the slope, because the mean is subtracted from each number, so even though the values change, the distance between then doesn’t thus keeping the slope the same. The estimated slope is beta = 0.973003. Higher Agreeableness decreases the the log-odds of being at or below each threshold, shifting values towards having higher Agreeableness values and higher slightly/moderately accurate values. The most likely response is Moderately accurate (0.3760365).

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
5.2 Interpreting Slope on Latent Scale
The slope on the latent logit scale is beta = 0.973003. The latent scale is a continuous scale which reflects the ease of making friends. Each one point increase in Agreeableness increases this latent scale of making friends by 0.973003.
The middle categories, being the adjacent thresholds, are each about 0.8006473, meaning that the one point of Agreeableness change alters their score on the latency continuum of making friends by 121.5270492%.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
6.1. Testing Proportional Odds
When using a model that assumes proportional odds, there is the same slope used with the five thresholds. Therefore, we can refit a model using nominal_test() with a different slope for the predictor (Agreeableness) at each threshold, and compares the models to compare the models and determine if it fits better. If the new slope does not fit significantly better than the old one, then they can all maintain the same slope.


Tests of nominal effects

formula: E4 ~ agree_c
        Df  logLik    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>     -4210.5 8432.9                
agree_c  4 -4209.7 8439.4 1.4773   0.8307


The LRT statistic is 1.477286, with 4 degrees of freedom, and finally with a p-value of 0.8306572. This means that the test is not significant, and therefore the shared slope may be used rather than an individual one for each threshold. If it was significant, we would have the fit a partial proportional odds model.

text:
7.1. Interpreting the Odds Ratio
Agreeableness The odds ratio found for my predictor of Agreeableness is e^beta = 2.6458781, with the 95% CI being [2.4364666, 2.8753943], and finally a p-value of 2.3433206^{-117}.
These results mean that each one-point increase in Agreeableness multiplies the odds of responding above a threshold by a 165%, which is an increase in odds. This is because the slope of each threshold is the same, so the odds between each of them would be the same.
